title: Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI Inference
story_key: story|title:together compiler continual compilation for ai inference
content_excerpt: 40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production... AI inference workloads are dynamic. There are thousands of regimes spanning new models, hardware platforms, customers, use cases, and traffic shapes. It’s no longer scalable to optimize each of these regimes by hand. Agents are a great fit for this problem, in theory. They can adapt to new workloads and search over the space of possible optimizations without relying on fixed rules or heuristics that plague human experts and traditional machine learning compilers. However, today’s agentic systems are bottlenecked by the speed of experimentation. In less than 24 hours, TKCC achieves up to 2.6x higher TPS across frontier open source models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1-Flash, DeepSeek v4.1-Flash), sets the state-of-the-art on SemiAnalysis’ InferenceX benchmark for low-latency with 1111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1-Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1-Flash, and outperforms available open-source megakernels by 1.7x on their workhorse Llama 1B batch size 1 setting. Furthermore, TKCC generalizes to domains beyond language model inference (weather modeling, PDE, time-series, and biology). This performance boost is enabled by TKCC’s 252x higher experiment throughput compared to baseline agentic performance optimization systems. Together Compiler is serving trillions of tokens today. As an inference provider, we see a variety of user behaviors based on regional patterns, new model releases, and burstiness. It’s clear that we must adapt to ever-changing user behavior with specialized optimizations for each new deployment. TKCC takes as input the traffic shape, model, and hardware. TKCC uses agents to generate a series of optimizations for an inference engine. 1. TKCC maximizes experimentation throughput and minimizes GPU idle time during agent optimization ‍ Most existing agentic inference optimization systems require agents to launch and teardown engines like VLLM, SGLang, or TRT-LLM to test each new experiment. However, engine start times are tens of minutes , significantly impeding experimentation throughput (see table below). Instead, TKCC proposes a new paradigm of “persistent engines” where the engine starts up once and can hot-reload any candidate forward pass, without any restarts. title: Baton – Keep long coding goals moving across AI coding agents
story_key: story|title:baton keep long coding goals moving across ai coding agents
content_excerpt: Relay a long coding goal across subscription agents without spending paid credits baton keeps one long coding goal moving for days by passing it between coding agents, stopping each one before it can spend money it should not. It works with Codex and Antigravity alone; Claude is an optional third, paid by use, that only joins the queue once you save an API key for it. Its turn ends at USD 50 or 5 hours, whichever comes first, it is left out of a goal after USD 150 spent in that goal, and the monthly ceiling stays above all of that. You give it a goal (an objective, a working directory and a verification command). It runs one agent until that agent nears its limit or its turn (5 hours) ends, hands the work to the next, and when every agent is out, sleeps until the earliest reset and carries on. It finishes only when the verification command exits 0; an agent saying "done" means nothing. Every agent runs through its vendor's own CLI. baton reimplements no agent. Context moves between them through the repository, its commits and a handoff file, and each vendor's own conversation is resumed when its turn comes again. Inside a goal the work follows a cycle of plan, build and review, with a strong and a working model per provider (see Phases ). How baton works: Codex, Antigravity and then Claude take turns; every goal runs plan, build and review, then the check, then consensus of every agent, and only then is it done. baton does not bring its own AI or its own methods. It drives tools you install, and works with two projects it did not write. Everything it depends on or works with: baton was tested with Codex CLI 0.166.0, Claude Code 2.1.318 and ai-memory 3.4.1. The stream formats and hook options it relies on are version-specific, so other versions may not behave the same. How the pieces fit. baton owns the rotation, the phases, the limits and the guards. Each vendor CLI (Codex, Antigravity, Claude Code) does the actual work, one round at a time, inside a model baton chose. Superpowers gives every round its method. ai-memory gives the goals long-term memory. OpenCode is the chat window in front of it all. Superpowers is not optional, and there is no setting to turn it off. No round runs without it: a goal that cannot find it waits, still running, and looks again every 5 minutes, so installing it is all that is needed. title: Frontier quality at 1% of the cost: a production benchmark of LLM classifiers
story_key: story|title:frontier quality at 1 of the cost a production benchmark of llm classifiers
content_excerpt: At Airbnb, we use AI models for classification tasks, such as detecting risky user-generated content, identifying why customers contact support, and recognizing topics in reviews. These tasks require subtle language understanding and the common sense to interpret what people leave unsaid. Frontier models, with hundreds of billions of parameters and internet-scale pretraining, are often good at these tasks. But for interactive products and high-volume workloads, accuracy is only part of the requirement. We also need low latency, manageable serving costs, and control over the tradeoff between false positives and false negatives. Smaller open-weight models are faster and cheaper to run at scale. By extracting logprobs, we’re able to produce a score for thresholding. But these small models are trained to handle a vast range of conversations and our tasks occupy just a tiny corner of that training distribution. Out of the box, they often miss subtle distinctions that matter immensely for our product. Better prompting has limits. (I’m often reminded of an assignment from elementary school: write instructions for how to make a PB&J. “Put the knife in the peanut butter,” you’d write, only to have the teacher stab through the jar or insert the handle instead of the blade. There seem to be no instructions detailed enough to avoid every possible lapse in common sense.) GLOWC, an internal framework used by engineers at Airbnb, makes it easy to fine-tune open-weight language (and vision-language) models into fast, accurate classifiers. In this blog post, we put one of these classifiers head-to-head with open-weight and proprietary models and find that it matches frontier-level quality in under 100ms at roughly 1% of the cost. Public benchmarks rarely capture a real product’s constraints. Instead, we test a production classifier that screens content for violations of Airbnb’s policy on pricing and payment transparency . The task requires recognizing subtle policy distinctions with high precision, since false positives prevent legitimate content from being published. The model is called thousands of times per minute, and because it gates publication in real time, a score must return within 200ms. title: StrataFlux: Memory-Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference
summary: Quantization reduces the memory and bandwidth demands of large language model (LLM) inference but can degrade accuracy; offloading higher-precision data can instead stall generation. We introduce StrataFlux, a framework that challenges this tradeoff by recovering accuracy lost to low-bit weight and key-value (KV) cache quantization while retaining quantization's memory and speed advantages. StrataFlux co-designs refinement representation, selection, and delivery to make host RAM and solid-state drives useful sources of additional precision. Its selective precision streaming reduces transfer volume, overlaps delivery with computation, and reuses fetched precision across decoding steps so generation need not wait for every transfer. We evaluate 2-4-bit weights and 2-3-bit KV-cache on dedicated GPUs and unified-memory platforms. For 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, StrataFlux reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while maintaining 95.4% of the quantized base's throughput on RTX 5090. With 2-bit weights and KV, StrataFlux raises Qwen3-8B's AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use. At 128K context, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 3-bit weights and 2-bit KV achieves comparable perplexity and speed to vLLM's 4-bit AWQ weights and 8-bit KV on RTX 5090, using approximately half the GPU memory. These results show that GPU-resident precision need not set the accuracy ceiling, nor offloading-tier latency dictate decoding speed.

title: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
story_key: story|title:toyblocks a controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
content_excerpt: Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails. To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure. Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control. Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks : an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking. ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training. Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments. Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2 , MolmoBot , and MolmoSpaces , ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain. As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain. title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout
summary: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.

title: How We Optimized Browser Use for Deep Agents
summary: We compared seven browser toolsets for Deep Agents, picked Stagehand from Browserbase, and tuned it with LangSmith traces and evals. Here's what we learned.
story_key: story|title:how we optimized browser use for deep agents
content_excerpt: Browser agents can now take on multi-step work that's painful and time-consuming for people. Personal agents like Instinct and Meta's Muse plan cross-country road trips, cancel unused subscriptions, and list cars for sale, all on sites with no public APIs. DataDome saw agentic browser requests jump 4.7x in September alone. Browser use helps in two places: actions an API can't cover, like using a website the agent wasn't set up for, and end-to-end testing of the web apps coding agents build. Either way, the agent needs two things: This post focuses on the tools, and on making them good enough that the agent uses the browser well. We set out to give agents in Managed Deep Agents a browser. We compared seven toolsets and picked the best one, Stagehand ( GitHub ) from Browserbase . Then we improved it based on what agents did in LangSmith traces, and validated every change with evals. The biggest lesson was how much room there is to improve an agent through tool design. Browser use toolsets come in a few forms: native tools, an MCP server , or a CLI the agent runs in a shell. Browser use poses two unique challenges for those tools: We iterated with the agent development lifecycle : run the agent on a benchmark, read its traces in LangSmith to see where it wasted steps or tokens, change the tool, and run evals to check that the change helped. Every run was a LangSmith experiment , so we could compare setups side by side and click from any number into the trace behind it. We had every harness return structured output (a JSON answer). That way a formatting slip, like a one-line reply to a task that asks for a table, didn't count against its browsing. We upstreamed that option to Browserbase's evals. We first held the model and tasks fixed and changed only the toolset. The seven toolsets differ in how the agent calls them: Every toolset passed between 78% and 90% of tasks, but cost and speed varied widely. The Stagehand tools passed the most (90%) for $1.98 in total, at a median 17.4 s per task. Playwright MCP passed 78% for $26.71, about 13x the cost, and took three times as long per task ( full results ). The gap held on harder tasks. On HardBench's 38 core tasks, Deep Agents passed 30 with Stagehand's code-writing run tool and 21 with Browserbase's command-style browse CLI, at three times the cost per task. Early browser tooling repurposed testing SDKs like Playwright . As Browserbase puts it, "Playwright was built for testing, we built Stagehand for your agent

title: Agent-R$^2$: Scaling Agents for Realistic Productivity Work via Real-Source Data Synthesis
summary: Large language models have made rapid progress in agentic reasoning and tool use, raising expectations for agents that can take over realistic productivity work from humans. However, current agents still struggle to finish such tasks, where success requires following long-horizon professional workflows, understanding heterogeneous file contexts, and producing usable deliverables under fine-grained requirements. A key bottleneck is the lack of scalable post-training data that reflects real work intent, authentic file environments, and deliverable-level evaluation. To close this gap, we introduce Agent-R$^2$, a $\textbf{r}$eal-source data synthesis framework that scales training data for $\textbf{r}$ealistic productivity work. Instead of relying on manually specified workflows or LLM-generated files, Agent-R$^2$ grounds synthesis throughout the pipeline in real occupational seeds, corpus-derived workflow evidence, and authentic web-sourced files. From 10k web-corpus candidates, Agent-R$^2$ distills 4k task instances that pair real multi-format attachments with fine-grained, deliverable-level rubrics. On this data, we train Agent-R$^2$-4B via supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning, improving both end-to-end productivity performance and file-grounded reasoning. Trained on only 4k instances, Agent-R$^2$-4B surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on both GDPval (51.0$\%$ vs. 48.0$\%$) and OfficeQA (14.8$\%$ vs. 13.8$\%$). Further analysis shows that Agent-R$^2$ mitigates shortcut behavior, where agents produce superficially plausible deliverables before sufficiently grounding, constructing, or verifying them, while promoting sustained exploration.

title: Polarity Classification with Multitask Learning Syntax Augmentation
summary: Sentiment Analysis (SA) is a fundamental NLP task concerned with the identification and categorization of subjective information in text. While lexicon-based methods offer transparency, they often struggle with linguistic phenomena such as negation and intensification. Syntactic parsing has been integrated into SA pipelines to address this, but conventional parsers introduce significant computational overhead. Recent work shows that reformulating dependency parsing as a Sequence Labeling (SEL) task can improve efficiency. We propose and compare two strategies for integrating syntactic knowledge into a neural sentiment analysis model under unified Multi-Task Learning (MTL). The first, Standard-MTL, jointly learns dependency parsing (via sequence labeling) and sentiment polarity classification using a shared encoder with two task-specific heads. The second, Contrastive-MTL, provides implicit syntactic guidance through a contrastive auxiliary objective and a syntax-biased attention pooling mechanism, without requiring explicit label prediction. Both rely on syntactic annotations during training and eliminate need for hand-crafted compositional rules or external parsing at inference. We evaluate eleven datasets spanning seven languages---the MARC corpus (English, Spanish, French, German) and seven datasets from SemEval-2022 Task 10 (English, Spanish, Norwegian, Basque, Catalan)---using four established SEL encodings. With the relative encoding, Contrastive-MTL outperforms a syntax-naive baseline on 10 of 11 datasets and surpasses the external rule-based pipeline (SELSP) that parses at inference on all six datasets where the latter applies, while being 1.5--9$\times$ faster at evaluation. Standard-MTL is more dataset- and encoding-dependent. These results show implicit syntactic supervision during training can match or exceed explicit parsing at inference without computational overhead.

title: vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for Kimi K3.1 Pro
summary: vLLM supports Kimi K3.1 Pro on day 0: sparse attention on a KDA hybrid, a packed KV cache with FP8 or NVFP4 latents and MXFP4 index keys, token-sharded prefill, decode context parallelism, and fused low-latency decode.
story_key: model:vllm|ver:3.1|variant:pro|title:vllm delivers day 0 support for kimi k3 1 pro
content_excerpt: Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot AI's most capable open-weight model: a 2.8T-parameter (104B active) multimodal MoE with a 1M-token context that matches the strongest closed-source models on coding, agentic and knowledge benchmarks. The main change is attention: K3.1 Pro adds Sparse Attention (DSA) to all 24 full-attention layers for efficiency. vLLM supports it on day 0 on NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, Google TPUs and Alibaba T-Head Zhenwu PPUs. Each sparse attention layer has a small indexer next to its MLA attention. The indexer keeps one FP8 key per token (132 bytes with its scale) and scores every earlier token for each query with 32 lightweight heads. Then it keeps the top 2,048 tokens. MLA attention then runs exactly, but only over those 2,048 tokens. DSA was introduced in DeepSeek-V3.2; our DeepSeek-V3.2 post covers the indexer in more detail. The payoff is largest in long-context decode, which is bound by memory bandwidth. Dense MLA reads 576 bytes of FP8 latent per context token per layer. DSA still scans the whole context, but only the 132-byte index keys. It then reads the full latent for just 2,048 tokens. At long context, that is about 23% of the bytes dense MLA reads per layer. Figure 1: Sparse attention (DSA) in Kimi K3.1 Pro. The indexer scores every past token, keeps the top 2,048, and every query head attends exactly over only those tokens' latents. Step through it. The index keys are a second per-token cache next to the MLA latent. Under tensor parallelism (TP) both are replicated on every GPU; KDA state is per request, as in K3. The latent and the index keys can be quantized independently. An NVFP4 latent alone already brings K3.1 Pro below K3 with FP8. Opt-in MXFP4 index keys fit 11% more tokens on top and make the indexer 10–20% faster at long context. With both, eight GB300 GPUs hold 1.7× as many tokens as with FP8, and DCP8 multiplies that by seven: about 36 full 1M-token contexts at once, against 3 for TP8 with FP8. Figure 2: Measured KV cache capacity on 8× GB300. Change the latent and index-key formats, the parallelism, or the context length to see how many full contexts fit. Each DSA layer stores two per-token caches of different widths: the MLA latent (576 bytes in FP8, 352 in NVFP4) and the index keys (132 bytes in FP8, 68 in MXFP4). Neither width is a multiple of the other. The 69 KDA layers each add a recurrent state per request that is much larger than one layer's page of tokens. title: Harness Engineering: What's Actually New (And What Isn't)
summary:
Harness engineering is the new name for everything around the model: tools, context, guardrails, telemetry. Carly Richmond, Senior Manager of Developer Advocacy at Elastic, shows what's genuinely new about building agents, and why most of the harness still rests on software engineering fundamentals you already know.

What we cover:
– What harness engineering is, and how it builds on prompt, context and loop engineering
– What's genuinely new: non-determinism, tool calling and models that change under your feet
– Why TDD evolves into AI agent evals, and when LLM-as-a-judge is the wrong tool
– Writing tool descriptions for agents the way you'd write an OpenAPI spec
– Telemetry, guardrails and security for an agent harness

Chapters:
00:00:00 - Introduction
00:02:26 - What is harness engineering?
00:04:45 - Prompt vs context vs harness vs loop engineering
00:06:33 - What's genuinely new about building agents
00:09:28 - Incremental changes, pipelines and testing
00:12:09 - From TDD to AI agent evals
00:14:04 - Context engineering and why LLMs get things wrong
00:17:41 - Tools, OpenAPI and agent orchestration
00:21:43 - Observability, security and guardrails for agents
00:28:12 - Key takeaway and audience Q&A

title: claude-code v2.1.318
summary:
What's changed

  • Added a record of your answer when Claude Code asks to turn on the mods it writes in a session
  • Added assume_role on mantle upstreams of the Claude apps gateway, for a role in another AWS account and for per-developer AWS cost attribution
  • Added an effort option to a mod's $.model.fork, so a quick side job can run at low whatever effort the session uses; the result reports the effort sent
  • Added the date a stored claude.ai sign-in ends to claude auth status (loginExpiresAt) and to claude -p JSON results (credential_expires_at)
  • Added a one-line stderr warning to claude -p text output, starting 10 days before a stored claude.ai sign-in ends
  • Fixed --continue sometimes losing the earlier conversation after a malformed tool call's retries ran out (regression in 2.1.314)
  • Fixed macOS sessions with many running Bash commands stalling while memory grew
  • Fixed permission prompts being answered by keys typed just after sending a message, or before a slow prompt appeared
  • Fixed /logout, claude auth logout and claude mcp remove reporting success, and changes to trust, consent or MCP settings being dropped with no word, when the config file could not be updated on a shared network home directory
  • Fixed jobs exiting with Not logged in when another terminal or host signs in again to the same account and organization on the same home
  • Fixed claude mcp add and remove writing the config without its lock: they now wait for it or exit 1, though another job's save can still replace a saved server
  • Fixed claude plugin commands exiting before a slow token refresh was saved, which could sign you out on the next run
  • Fixed claude plugin validate passing a custom-named marketplace file that claude plugin marketplace add rejects
  • Fixed stdio MCP servers that exit on the version probe being re-probed on every start; a server that dies in under 3s for its own reason is also pinned to the legacy handshake for 7 days
  • Fixed sessions being refused at startup by an allowedProviders list that another login on the same machine had stored
  • Fixed idle compaction replacing a conversation with a reply that was not a summary
  • Fixed the "Now using usage credits" notice reappearing about every 30 seconds while a background subagent is running
  • Fixed custom slash commands that fail, or that only Claude can invoke, printing nothing in claude -p and SDK sessions
  • Fixed claude -p and Agent SDK sessions reporting success when an API error cut off a reply while a mod hooked turn.step
  • Fixed a message sent right after a model change still running after Stop in headless sessions: Stop now cancels or stops it as it would a queued message
  • Fixed a deleted session transcript being re-created with its last prompt when an idle non-interactive session exited
  • Fixed claude remote-control hosts, the background daemon and self-hosted runners failing to start new sessions (spawn ENOENT) after an update or version cleanup removed the binary of a still-running process
  • Fixed a running Claude Code process owned by another user (for example one left by sudo claude) being treated as dead by version cleanup, which could delete its binary
  • Fixed /remote-control showing a session as available after a failed connection
  • Fixed /design revoke reporting success when the request failed with a 404
  • Fixed a shell command approved after a self-hosted runner or cloud session restart running in the session's start folder, not the folder it was asked in; if that folder can't be entered, it is not run
  • Fixed Claude not being told when an approved connector tool was unavailable after a cloud session restart
  • Fixed cloud sessions being stopped in the middle of a turn when the service refuses uploads for several minutes
  • Fixed variables a Setup hook writes to CLAUDE_ENV_FILE not reaching the Bash tool in some cloud sessions
  • Fixed the iPhone app showing a cloud session's turn as finished while it kept running, after a response was cut off at a tool call or a refused image or document was removed
  • Fixed a restarted session re-sending a message that failed with an API error, ahead of the newer message waiting behind it
  • Fixed a restarted session dropping its interrupted turn when the restart came right after Claude read a large image or retried a tool call
  • Fixed every connection failing when the NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS file is empty, not PEM, or starts with a damaged certificate: readable certificates are now used, with a warning on stderr
  • Fixed workflows re-running finished agents when resumed after a usage limit
  • Fixed /mcp in cloud sessions counting tools the model can't use; a server's row now shows how many of its tools are available
  • Fixed a duplicate notification when Claude left the status field out of a PushNotification call
  • Fixed the error for a too-large image in a request with more than 20 images always saying the limit was 2000px; it now shows the API's limit
  • Fixed the runtime in background shell details not updating while the dialog is open
  • Fixed a mod's turn.step hook making a stopped reply finish as a success in headless runs
  • Fixed retention cleanup leaving a home that only runs claude -p with no ~/.claude.json backup: it now takes a fresh backup before deleting the last good one
  • Fixed the stored login being replaced by an empty file when a network home directory has no room left for data but still takes new files
  • Fixed tokens from setup-token being refused at start on machines with forceLoginOrgUUID, when the token belongs to a permitted organization
  • Fixed non-interactive launches replacing a ~/.claude.json that isn't valid JSON with defaults; the start now fails, says how to restore the file, and leaves it as is (#87551)
  • Fixed an empty ~/.claude.json with no backup being reported as corrupted; Claude Code now starts as it does when the file is missing
  • Fixed the restore command printed for a damaged or missing ~/.claude.json naming an empty or cut-off backup, or failing on a read-only file
  • Fixed the sign-in failure when a stored claude.ai login reaches its time limit: it now says so, and in claude -p names claude auth login and claude setup-token
  • Improved how ~/.claude.json, settings files and the stored login survive saves on shared network home directories: they are less often deleted, briefly emptied or replaced by a near-empty or older copy
  • Improved sessions on network file systems to look again when the configuration file is wrongly reported as missing, so fewer start without your MCP servers and trusted folders
  • Improved MCP tool errors: a call made before the tool is loaded now returns its input schema
  • Improved the reliability of git commits and pull request creation when the Bash tool runs macOS's built-in /bin/bash
  • Improved "Ask your admin for more usage" in the usage limit menu to send the request in one step
  • Improved how fast remote sessions reconnect after a pause or sleep
  • Improved You should know toasts to say "try again" instead of "press 2", which only works in the terminal
  • Improved auto-update reliability: a brief network failure while verifying a release is now retried right away instead of waiting for the next check
  • Improved unattended runs (claude -p, SDK apps) to stop rewriting ~/.claude.json on every run when nothing in it changed
  • Changed Claude Code to no longer install or update the IDE extension when started in an IDE terminal; use /ide from an outside terminal or your editor's extensions view
  • Changed subagents to stop instead of switching models when "Switch models when a message is flagged" is set to "Ask each time"
  • Changed background subagents to move a shell command to the background after 3 minutes on all providers, so the prompt cache doesn't expire while it runs
  • Changed subagent progress summaries on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, or with telemetry off: on a cold prompt cache, one can now wait up to 5 minutes for the subagent's pending response
  • Changed what a mod attaches at prompt.submit to stay in the user's turn rather than go out as a system message
  • Changed deniedMcpServers URL entries to also block Anthropic-provided servers whose upstream URL matches, and connectors in cloud sessions and on self-hosted runners, where the session is given the connector's own URL; otherwise deny a connector by name
  • Changed the /permissions rule details, built-in rules and delete confirmation views to use the standard dialog; pressing Ctrl+C twice there now goes back or cancels instead of quitting
  • Changed /claude-api managed-agents-onboard to give a new agent's built-in tools, and a quickstart template's MCP tools, the auto permission policy ("Judge risky actions") by default, matching the Claude Console; say "run without asking" to opt out
  • Removed the 2.1.288 fix that kept the model's earlier thinking when resuming a conversation started on 2.1.286 or earlier; that thinking can now be dropped
  • Gateway: Added a log warning when the Google access token from a federation (external_account) credentials file is about to expire
  • Gateway: Improved the log hints about listen.trusted_proxies: they now say to list only a proxy that adds the connecting address to X-Forwarded-For itself
  • Gateway: Improved the warning when AWS CountTokens fails on Amazon Bedrock: it says Claude Code, not the gateway, counts after the 501, and points at IAM only when AWS denies access
  • Self-hosted runner: Added CLAUDE_RUNNER_SPAWN_REASON to the orchestrator's spawn-runner hook environment: why Anthropic sent the request (e.g. runner_lost, resumed); unset when none was sent
  • Self-hosted runner: Added a startup warning when --release-idle-session-min is the last argument with no value (still ignored) or has a value of only spaces (still read as 0)
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed the orchestrator's log lines: ok session=… now prints at every log level on stdout (was debug only, stderr) with reason=… after jti=…, and nack session=… ends its fields with reason=… after retryable=…; update scripts that match retryable=true: or retryable=false:
  • Remote Control: Fixed a misleading "spawn error: ENOENT" when a session's working folder is missing; the error now names the folder
  • Remote Control: Improved the title a fork of a terminal fork is created with when the app doesn't set one: "Name (fork 2)"
  • [VSCode] Fixed a window whose sign-in the organization's settings refuse starting a new Claude Code process in the background every minute
  • [VSCode] Fixed a long word in the chat panel's error banner pushing its close button out of view
  • [VSCode] Improved the sign-in screen to show what Claude Code printed when its sign-in status check fails
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a No repository option: a cloud session on an Anthropic-hosted environment can now start without picking a repository
  • [Cloud sessions] Added the usual Chrome names to cloud sessions, so tools other than Playwright can find the built-in Chromium through google-chrome and CHROME_PATH
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a New session button to the card shown when a cloud session's environment was deleted, where the message box is hidden
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed reading GitHub Actions logs in cloud sessions: gh run view --log and gh api log requests now get the log in most environments, not an unreachable redirect
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved most Create PR failure messages in cloud and Remote Control sessions: they now give the reason or a link to GitHub instead of saying Try again
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed connector search results to tell Claude that the search covers only part of the connector directory
  • [Remote Control] Fixed side-by-side checkouts of one repository looking identical in the environment menu's Remote Control rows; each now shows its own folder name
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed keyboard focus and screen reader announcements in Claude Tag admin setup; pressing Escape in the connect form no longer also closes the Add dialog
  • [Code Review] Improved the Code Review analytics page to retry once after a server or network failure, then show a Try again banner instead of empty cards

title: claude-agent-sdk-python v0.2.177
summary:
New Features

  • on_failure option for HookMatcher: Control what happens when a hook callback fails. Set on_failure="block" to block the action when a callback raises, returns None, or returns a value the CLI rejects. Defaults to "continue" (treat failure as no decision). Requires a CLI version that supports this option; connecting to an older CLI with on_failure="block" raises CLIConnectionError (#1460)

Internal/Other Changes

  • Updated bundled Claude CLI to version 2.1.317
  • Tests: e2e tests now accept either Bash or PowerShell tool in shell-dependent tests, fixing intermittent failures on Windows (#1467)

PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/claude-agent-sdk/0.2.177/
